docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
The quantum computing era is approaching. While cryptographically-relevant quantum computers (CRQCs) capable of breaking today’s public-key cryptography do not yet exist, their eventual arrival is now widely considered a matter of when, not if. The consequences are severe: every public-key cryptosystem in use today — RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ECDH, ECDSA — would be broken by Shor’s algorithm running on a CRQC.

Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is the field developing new cryptographic algorithms that resist both classical and quantum attacks. After an eight-year standardization process, NIST published the first three PQC standards in August 2024 (FIPS 203, 204, 205), and selected a fifth algorithm (HQC) in March 2025. The migration from classical to quantum-safe cryptography is now an organizational imperative.

This book provides a thorough technical treatment of PQC, covering:

  • Mathematical foundations: Lattice problems, learning with errors, code-based cryptography.

  • Algorithm families: Lattice-based, code-based, hash-based, multivariate, isogeny-based.

  • NIST standards: FIPS 203/204/205 and upcoming algorithms.

  • Implementation: Software libraries (liboqs, PQClean), hardware (NTT ASIC, GPU), embedded systems.

  • Migration strategy: Cryptographic inventory, hybrid deployment, PKI transition.

  • Side-channel attacks: Power analysis, timing attacks, fault injection, and defenses.

  • Applications: TLS, messaging, PKI, code signing, blockchain.

  • National solutions: NIST, NSA, German BSI, French ANSSI, Korean KPQC, Chinese SM, Russian GOST.

The “Harvest Now, Decrypt Later” threat means action is required today, not after CRQCs arrive.

docs.title: 1.1 The Quantum Threat to Classical Cryptography
docs.text:
Modern digital security rests on a small set of mathematical problems that are computationally intractable for classical computers. Public-key cryptography — the backbone of secure internet communication — relies on:

  • Integer Factorization: Breaking RSA requires factoring large semiprimes (e.g., RSA-2048).

  • Discrete Logarithm Problem (DLP): Breaking Diffie-Hellman and DSA over finite fields.

  • Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP): Breaking ECDH and ECDSA.

These problems are hard for classical computers, requiring sub-exponential to exponential time. Quantum computers change this landscape fundamentally.

Shor’s Algorithm — The Existential Threat

Peter Shor’s 1994 quantum algorithm solves integer factorization and discrete logarithm in polynomial time \(O((\log N)^3)\) on a quantum computer. This breaks RSA, Diffie-Hellman, DSA, ECDH, and ECDSA completely. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) running Shor’s algorithm would render all currently deployed public-key cryptography useless.

docs.title: 1.1.1 Grover’s Algorithm and Symmetric Cryptography
docs.text:
Grover’s 1996 algorithm provides a quadratic speedup for unstructured search problems, impacting symmetric cryptography:

Table 1.1. Impact of Quantum Algorithms on Cryptographic Primitives Primitive Classical Security Quantum Security Action RSA-2048 112 bits Broken (Shor) Replace ECDH P-256 128 bits Broken (Shor) Replace ECDSA P-384 192 bits Broken (Shor) Replace DH-3072 128 bits Broken (Shor) Replace AES-128 128 bits 64 bits (Grover) Upgrade to AES-256 AES-256 256 bits 128 bits (Grover) Retain SHA-256 256 bits 128 bits (Grover) Retain (collision resistance halved) SHA-384 384 bits 192 bits (Grover) Retain SHA-3 256 bits 128 bits (Grover) Retain

What Grover Means for AES

Grover’s algorithm reduces the effective key length of AES-128 from 128 bits to 64 bits — insufficient for long-term security. AES-128 should be upgraded to AES-256 in quantum-resilient deployments. AES-256 retains 128-bit quantum security, which is acceptable per NIST guidelines.

docs.title: 1.1.2 The “Harvest Now, Decrypt Later” (HNDL) Threat
docs.text:
One of the most urgent concerns in PQC migration is HNDL (also called “Store Now, Decrypt Later”):

  1. An adversary intercepts and stores encrypted data today (e.g., VPN traffic, TLS sessions).

  2. When a CRQC becomes available (estimates: 5–20 years), the adversary decrypts the stored ciphertext.

  3. Data with long-term sensitivity (state secrets, health records, financial data, trade secrets) is compromised retroactively.

HNDL Timeline Urgency

Even if CRQCs arrive in 2035, data encrypted with RSA/ECDH today — in 2025 — can be stored and later decrypted. Any data requiring confidentiality beyond 10 years must be protected with PQC now. NIST, NSA (CNSA 2.0), and BSI all emphasize the urgency of the HNDL threat.

docs.title: 1.2.1 Lattice Theory
docs.text:
A lattice \(\mathcal{L}\) is a discrete additive subgroup of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Given a basis matrix \(\mathbf{B} = [\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, …, \mathbf{b}_n] \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\), the lattice is:

\[\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{B}) = \left\{ \mathbf{B}\mathbf{x} \;\middle|\; \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{Z}^n \right\} = \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \mathbf{b}_i \;\middle|\; x_i \in \mathbb{Z} \right\}\]

Definition 1.1 (Shortest Vector Problem (SVP))

Given a lattice \(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{B})\), find the shortest non-zero vector \(\mathbf{v} \in \mathcal{L}\) such that \(\|\mathbf{v}\|\) is minimized. SVP is NP-hard in general and conjectured to be hard even for quantum computers.

Definition 1.2 (Closest Vector Problem (CVP))

Given a lattice \(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{B})\) and a target vector \(\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^n\), find the lattice point closest to \(\mathbf{t}\): \(\arg\min_{\mathbf{v} \in \mathcal{L}} \|\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{t}\|\). CVP is also NP-hard.

docs.title: 1.2.2 Learning With Errors (LWE)
docs.text:
LWE, introduced by Regev in 2005, is the computational foundation of most deployed PQC algorithms.

Definition 1.3 (Learning With Errors (LWE))

Let \(n, q\) be integers and \(\chi\) be an error distribution over \(\mathbb{Z}_q\). The LWE problem: given \(m\) samples \((\mathbf{a}_i, b_i) \in \mathbb{Z}_q^n \times \mathbb{Z}_q\) where \(b_i = \langle \mathbf{a}_i, \mathbf{s} \rangle + e_i \pmod{q}\) with \(\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{Z}_q^n\) (secret) and \(e_i \leftarrow \chi\) (small error), find \(\mathbf{s}\).

The LWE problem is computationally equivalent (via quantum reduction) to worst-case lattice problems.

Example 1.1 (Small LWE Instance)

Let \(n=4\), \(q=17\), \(\mathbf{s} = (3, 1, 4, 1)\). Three LWE samples:

\[(5, 2, 11, 3) \cdot (3,1,4,1)^T + (-1) = 15+2+44+3-1 \equiv 12 \pmod{17}\]

The error term \(e = -1\) is small relative to \(q=17\).

docs.title: 1.2.3 Ring-LWE and Module-LWE
docs.text:
Ring-LWE (RLWE) works over the polynomial ring \(R_q = \mathbb{Z}_q[X]/(X^n+1)\) where \(n\) is a power of 2. This allows efficient operations using the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT).

Module-LWE (MLWE) generalizes RLWE to module lattices over \(R_q^k\) for dimension \(k\). ML-KEM and ML-DSA use MLWE. Parameters:

Table 1.2. LWE Variants Comparison Variant Ring Key Operations Performance Examples LWE \(\mathbb{Z}_q^n\) Matrix-vector Slow Regev, FrodoKEM RLWE \(R_q = \mathbb{Z}_q[X]/(X^n+1)\) Polynomial Fast (NTT) NTRU, early Kyber MLWE \(R_q^k\) Module-poly Very Fast ML-KEM, ML-DSA

docs.title: 1.2.4 Number Theoretic Transform (NTT)
docs.text:
The NTT is the discrete Fourier transform over \(\mathbb{Z}_q\), enabling fast polynomial multiplication in \(O(n \log n)\) rather than \(O(n^2)\).

Definition 1.4 (NTT)

For \(q\) prime with \(q \equiv 1 \pmod{2n}\), let \(\omega\) be a primitive \(2n\)-th root of unity in \(\mathbb{Z}_q\). The NTT of \(\mathbf{a} = (a_0, …, a_{n-1})\) is:

\[\hat{a}_k = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} a_j \omega^{jk} \pmod{q}, \quad k = 0, 1, …, n-1\]

Polynomial multiplication then reduces to pointwise multiplication in the NTT domain: \(\hat{c}_k = \hat{a}_k \cdot \hat{b}_k\), followed by inverse NTT.

For ML-KEM with \(n=256\), \(q=3329\), \(\omega = 17\) (primitive 512th root of unity mod 3329). The NTT reduces polynomial multiplication from \(\sim\)65,536 multiplications to \(\sim\)3,328 multiplications plus the NTT overhead.

docs.title: 1.2.5 Short Integer Solution (SIS)
docs.text:
The SIS problem underlies many signature schemes:

Definition 1.5 (SIS Problem)

Given a matrix \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{Z}_q^{n \times m}\), find a short non-zero vector \(\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{Z}^m\) such that \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{0} \pmod{q}\) and \(\|\mathbf{z}\| \leq \beta\).

SIS is as hard as worst-case lattice problems (via average-case to worst-case reduction).

docs.title: 1.2.6 Code-Based Mathematical Foundations
docs.text:
Linear error-correcting codes provide an alternative hard problem family:

Definition 1.6 (Syndrome Decoding Problem (SDP))

Given a parity-check matrix \(\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{(n-k) \times n}\), a syndrome \(\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{n-k}\), and a weight bound \(w\), find \(\mathbf{e} \in \mathbb{F}_2^n\) with Hamming weight \(\text{wt}(\mathbf{e}) \leq w\) such that \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{e}^T = \mathbf{s}\). SDP is NP-complete.

docs.title: 1.2.7 Hash-Based Security
docs.text: Hash-based schemes rely solely on the security of the underlying hash function (e.g., SHA-256, SHAKE-256), making them quantum-resistant via Grover’s algorithm analysis: an \(n\)-bit preimage search takes \(O(2^{n/2})\) quantum operations (acceptable for \(n=256\)).

docs.title: 1.3 Security Levels
docs.text:
NIST defines five security levels for PQC algorithms:

Table 1.3. NIST PQC Security Levels Level Classical Classical Equivalent Quantum Equivalent 1 AES-128 exhaustive key search 128-bit (classical) 64-bit (Grover) 2 SHA-256/SHA3-256 collision 128-bit collision 85-bit quantum collision 3 AES-192 exhaustive key search 192-bit 96-bit 4 SHA-384/SHA3-384 collision 192-bit collision 128-bit quantum collision 5 AES-256 exhaustive key search 256-bit 128-bit

Security Level Selection

Security Level 1 (ML-KEM-512) is adequate for most applications. Classified/government data often requires Level 3 or 5. The NSA CNSA 2.0 mandates Level 5 (ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-87) for classified national security systems.

docs.title: 1.4.1 Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM)
docs.text:
A KEM is a three-algorithm system:

Algorithm: KEM Abstract Syntax

  1. \((\mathit{ek}, \mathit{dk}) \leftarrow \textsc{KeyGen}()\) // Encapsulation key (public) + Decapsulation key (private)

  2. \((\mathit{K}, \mathit{c}) \leftarrow \textsc{Encaps}(\mathit{ek})\) // Shared secret \(K\) + Ciphertext \(c\)

  3. \(\mathit{K}' \leftarrow \textsc{Decaps}(\mathit{dk}, \mathit{c})\) // Recover shared secret; \(K' = K\) if valid

KEMs replace public-key encryption in key establishment. The shared secret \(K\) is used to derive symmetric keys via a KDF (e.g., HKDF).

docs.title: 1.4.2 Digital Signature Scheme (DSS)
docs.text:
Algorithm: Digital Signature Scheme Abstract Syntax

  1. \((\mathit{pk}, \mathit{sk}) \leftarrow \textsc{KeyGen}()\) // Verification key (public) + Signing key (private)

  2. \(\sigma \leftarrow \textsc{Sign}(\mathit{sk}, M)\) // Signature \(\sigma\) over message \(M\)

  3. \(b \leftarrow \textsc{Verify}(\mathit{pk}, M, \sigma)\) // Accept (\(b=1\)) or Reject (\(b=0\))

docs.title: 1.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Shor’s algorithm breaks RSA, DH, ECDH, and ECDSA in polynomial quantum time — replacing these is mandatory.

  • Grover’s algorithm halves the effective key length of symmetric ciphers — upgrade AES-128 to AES-256.

  • The HNDL threat is immediate: encrypted data collected today can be decrypted when CRQCs arrive.

  • PQC security rests on hard mathematical problems: SVP/CVP (lattices), SDP (codes), MQ (multivariate), and hash function properties.

  • NIST finalized FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) in August 2024; HQC selected as the 5th algorithm in March 2025.

  • Security levels 1–5 correspond to AES-128 through AES-256 equivalent quantum security.

docs.title: 2.1 Lattice-Based Cryptography
docs.text: Lattice-based schemes are the most deployed PQC family, forming the basis of three of the four current NIST standards.

docs.title: 2.1.1 ML-KEM (FIPS 203) — Module-Lattice KEM
docs.text: ML-KEM (formerly CRYSTALS-Kyber) is the primary NIST KEM standard. It is based on the Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) problem over the ring \(R_q = \mathbb{Z}_q[X]/(X^{256}+1)\) with \(q=3329\).

docs.title: ML-KEM Key Generation
docs.text:
Algorithm: ML-KEM KeyGen (simplified)

  1. Sample \(\mathbf{A} \in R_q^{k \times k}\) from a seed (XOF/SHAKE-128)

  2. Sample secret \(\mathbf{s} \in R_q^k\) with small coefficients (\(\eta_1\)-CBD)

  3. Sample error \(\mathbf{e} \in R_q^k\) with small coefficients (\(\eta_1\)-CBD)

  4. Compute public key: \(\mathbf{t} = \text{NTT}(\mathbf{A}) \circ \text{NTT}(\mathbf{s}) + \text{NTT}(\mathbf{e})\)

  5. return \((\mathit{ek} = (\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{t}), \;\mathit{dk} = \mathbf{s})\)

docs.title: 2.1.2 ML-DSA (FIPS 204) — Module-Lattice Digital Signature Algorithm
docs.text: ML-DSA (formerly CRYSTALS-Dilithium) is based on the hardness of MLWE and Module-SIS over \(R_q = \mathbb{Z}_q[X]/(X^{256}+1)\) with \(q = 8380417\).

docs.title: ML-DSA Sign/Verify
docs.text:
Algorithm: ML-DSA Sign (Fiat-Shamir with Aborts, simplified)

  1. \(\mathbf{A} \leftarrow\) ExpandA(\(\rho\)); \(\mathbf{s}_1, \mathbf{s}_2 \leftarrow\) small vectors from private seed

  2. Compute \(\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_1 + \mathbf{s}_2\); \((\mathbf{t}_1, \mathbf{t}_0) \leftarrow\) Power2Round(\(\mathbf{t}\))

  3. repeat

    • Sample masking vector \(\mathbf{y}\) with coefficients in \((-\gamma_1, \gamma_1]\)

    • \(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}\); \(\mathbf{w}_1 = \text{HighBits}(\mathbf{w})\)

    • \(c = H(\mu \| \mathbf{w}_1)\) // Challenge hash

    • \(\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{y} + c\mathbf{s}_1\) // Response vector

    • if \(\|\mathbf{z}\|_\infty \geq \gamma_1 - \beta\) or hints needed \(> \omega\) then

      • continue // Rejection sampling — restart

  4. until conditions met

  5. return \(\sigma = (c, \mathbf{z}, \text{hints})\)

docs.title: 2.1.3 FN-DSA (FIPS 206) — Falcon
docs.text:
FN-DSA (FALCON) uses NTRU lattices with a Gaussian sampler for lattice-based signatures. It achieves significantly smaller signatures than ML-DSA but requires floating-point arithmetic, posing implementation challenges.

Table 2.4. FN-DSA (FALCON) Parameter Sets Variant Level pk (B) sk (B) sig (B) FALCON-512 1 897 1281 \(\sim\)666 FALCON-1024 5 1793 2305 \(\sim\)1280

FALCON Implementation Challenges

FALCON’s Gaussian sampler requires high-precision floating-point arithmetic. This creates significant side-channel risks: timing variations and floating-point exceptions can leak secret information. Constant-time FP implementations are non-trivial. Use ML-DSA (FIPS 204) for general use cases; FN-DSA is preferred only when signature size is critical.

docs.title: 2.2 Code-Based Cryptography
docs.text: Code-based cryptography has the longest security track record in PQC, dating to McEliece’s 1978 scheme.

docs.title: 2.2.1 Classic McEliece
docs.text: Classic McEliece uses binary Goppa codes, which are a family of algebraic codes with efficient decoding algorithms. The security relies on the difficulty of decoding a random linear code (the Syndrome Decoding Problem, NP-complete).

docs.title: McEliece Construction
docs.text:
1. Setup: Choose a binary Goppa code \(\mathcal{G}\) with parameters \([n, k, t]\) (length \(n\), dimension \(k\), error-correcting capacity \(t\)). Generate a parity-check matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) and an efficient decoder.

  2. Public Key: A randomized generator matrix \(\mathbf{G}' = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{P}\) (where \(\mathbf{S}\) is a secret non-singular matrix, \(\mathbf{G}\) is the Goppa code generator, \(\mathbf{P}\) is a permutation matrix).

  3. Encryption: \(c = m\mathbf{G}' + e\) where \(e\) has weight \(\leq t\).

  4. Decryption: Use \(\mathbf{S}^{-1}\) and \(\mathbf{P}^{-1}\) to transform \(c\), then run the Goppa decoder.

docs.title: 2.2.2 HQC — The 5th NIST Algorithm
docs.text:
Hamming Quasi-Cyclic (HQC), selected by NIST in March 2025 as the fifth PQC standard, is a code-based KEM with much more practical key sizes than Classic McEliece.

HQC is based on the Decisional QC-LRPC (Low Rank Parity Check) decoding problem in the Hamming metric over quasi-cyclic codes.

docs.title: HQC Construction Overview
docs.text:
HQC encodes messages using Reed-Muller codes composed with Reed-Solomon codes for efficient error correction, then adds quasi-cyclic structure to reduce key sizes.

Algorithm: HQC Encapsulation (simplified)

  1. Public key: \((h, \mathbf{s}) \in R \times R\) where \(R = \mathbb{F}_2[X]/(X^n-1)\)

  2. Sample message \(m\); compute \((\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2) \leftarrow G(m)\)

  3. \(\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{r}_1 + h \cdot \mathbf{r}_2\) // Quasi-cyclic structure

  4. \(\mathbf{v} = m\mathcal{C} + \mathbf{s} \cdot \mathbf{r}_2 + \mathbf{e}_2\) // Encode message with error

  5. Shared key \(K = H(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, m)\)

  6. return \(((K, (\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})))\)

docs.title: 2.3 Hash-Based Cryptography
docs.text: Hash-based signatures derive their security entirely from the collision resistance and one-wayness of the underlying hash function, making them the most “conservative” post-quantum signature choice.

docs.title: 2.3.1 Lamport One-Time Signature
docs.text:
The foundational idea: for each message bit, include either the preimage for 0 or the preimage for 1.

  1. KeyGen: For each of \(n\) message bits, sample two random values \((x_i^0, x_i^1)\). Public key: \((H(x_i^0), H(x_i^1))\).

  2. Sign: For message bit \(m_i\), release \(x_i^{m_i}\).

  3. Verify: Check \(H(x_i^{m_i}) = pk_i^{m_i}\).

Limitation: each keypair can only be used once. Winternitz OTS (W-OTS+) amortizes this across \(w\) bits.

docs.title: 2.3.2 SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) — SPHINCS+
docs.text:
SLH-DSA is a stateless hash-based signature scheme using a hypertree structure of XMSS (extended Merkle signature scheme) trees.

Figure 2.1. SLH-DSA hypertree structure: \(d\) layers of Merkle trees with FORS at leaves. Table 2.7. SLH-DSA Parameter Sets (FIPS 205) — Selected Variant Level Hash pk (B) sk (B) sig (B) Sign (ms) SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s 1 SHA-256 32 64 7856 \(\sim\)1200 SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f 1 SHA-256 32 64 17088 \(\sim\)15 SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s 1 SHAKE-256 32 64 7856 \(\sim\)2200 SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128f 1 SHAKE-256 32 64 17088 \(\sim\)26 SLH-DSA-SHA2-256s 5 SHA-512 64 128 29792 \(\sim\)20000 SLH-DSA-SHA2-256f 5 SHA-512 64 128 49856 \(\sim\)130

The “s” (small) variants minimize signature size at the cost of signing time; “f” (fast) variants sign quickly but have larger signatures.

SLH-DSA Advantages

  • Conservative security: Only assumes hash function security (no novel math)

  • Tiny public key: Only 32 bytes (smallest of any PQC scheme)

  • Stateless: No state management required (unlike XMSS/LMS)

  • Quantum-safe by design: Hash security well-understood against Grover

SLH-DSA Limitations

SLH-DSA has slow signing (up to 20 seconds for -256s) and very large signatures (up to 50 KB). It is best used for code signing, certificate authorities, and other low-frequency signing operations where signature size and speed are not critical.

docs.title: 2.3.3 Stateful Hash-Based Signatures: XMSS and LMS
docs.text:
XMSS (RFC 8391) and LMS (RFC 8554) are stateful alternatives, providing smaller signatures but requiring careful state management (the same key must never be reused).

Table 2.8. Stateful vs Stateless Hash-Based Signatures Scheme Stateful? Sig size Speed Use case SLH-DSA No 8–50 KB Slow (sign) General, CA, code sign XMSS Yes 2–3 KB Faster Firmware, HSM LMS Yes 2–4 KB Faster IoT, embedded

docs.title: 2.4 Multivariate Cryptography
docs.text:
Multivariate schemes base security on the MQ problem: solving a system of multivariate quadratic equations over a finite field.

Definition 2.1 (MQ Problem)

Given \(m\) quadratic polynomials \(f_1, …, f_m \in \mathbb{F}_q[x_1, …, x_n]\), find \((a_1, …, a_n) \in \mathbb{F}_q^n\) such that \(f_i(a_1, …, a_n) = 0\) for all \(i\). The MQ problem is NP-hard for \(m \approx n\).

docs.title: 2.4.1 Oil and Vinegar Construction
docs.text:
The Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) scheme remains a promising construction after the collapse of Rainbow:

  1. Setup: Partition variables into “oil” (\(o\) variables) and “vinegar” (\(v\) variables).

  2. Public key: A system of \(o\) quadratic polynomials mixing both types.

  3. Private trapdoor: The separation of oil and vinegar variables allows efficient inversion.

  4. Sign: Fix vinegar variables randomly; solve for oil variables (linear system).

Rainbow NIST Withdrawal

Rainbow, a multivariate signature scheme that reached Round 3 of NIST’s competition, was broken in 2022 by Ward Beullens using a “rectangular MinRank attack” that required only 53 CPU hours to recover the private key from a Rainbow III (Level 3) public key. This highlights that multivariate schemes remain an active research area with ongoing security analysis.

docs.title: 2.5 Isogeny-Based Cryptography
docs.text: Isogeny-based schemes use maps (isogenies) between elliptic curves as one-way functions. After the 2022 SIDH/SIKE break, the field has pivoted to new constructions.

docs.title: 2.5.1 The SIDH/SIKE Collapse
docs.text:
SIKE (Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsulation) was a NIST Round 4 finalist based on the SIDH problem. In July 2022, Castryck and Decru published a devastating attack that recovered SIKE private keys in just 62 CPU minutes using classical computers, based on exploiting auxiliary points that SIDH was required to reveal.

SIDH/SIKE is Broken

SIKE was completely broken by a classical attack in 2022. Do not use SIKE or SIDH for any application. The Castryck-Decru attack used torsion point information to recover secret isogenies via a “glue-and-split” technique over abelian surfaces.

docs.title: 2.7 Summary
docs.text:
• ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is the primary PQC KEM: fast, compact, based on MLWE.

  • ML-DSA (FIPS 204) is the general-purpose PQC signature; prefers over FN-DSA for most applications.

  • FN-DSA (FIPS 206) offers smaller signatures but complex constant-time implementation.

  • SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) is the conservative hash-based signature; ideal for long-lived keys and CAs.

  • HQC is the 5th NIST algorithm (code-based KEM), selected March 2025, providing backup to lattice-based schemes.

  • Rainbow was broken in 2022 — never use it; UOV variants remain under active research.

  • SIKE/SIDH were broken by a classical attack in 2022 — never use them.

  • SQIsign and CSIDH represent promising isogeny-based constructions but remain pre-standard.

docs.title: 3.1 Overview of Finalized Standards
docs.text:
NIST finalized the first three Post-Quantum Cryptography standards in August 2024 after an eight-year standardization process. These represent the mandatory baseline for quantum-safe cryptography in U.S. government systems and are being adopted globally.

The Four Published NIST PQC Standards

  • FIPS 203 (August 2024): ML-KEM — Module-Lattice Key Encapsulation Mechanism

  • FIPS 204 (August 2024): ML-DSA — Module-Lattice Digital Signature Algorithm

  • FIPS 205 (August 2024): SLH-DSA — Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm

  • HQC (March 2025): Code-based KEM — 5th algorithm, draft standard pending

A draft standard for FIPS 206 (FN-DSA, based on FALCON) is expected in 2025–2026.

docs.title: 3.2.1 Specification Summary
docs.text:
FIPS 203 standardizes ML-KEM, derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber. Key design choices:

  • Module dimension \(k \in \{2, 3, 4\}\) (for ML-KEM-512/768/1024).

  • Ring \(R_q = \mathbb{Z}_{3329}[X]/(X^{256}+1)\); \(q = 3329\) chosen for efficient NTT.

  • Uses Kyber.CPA-PKE as an internal primitive, then applies the Fujisaki-Okamoto (FO) transform to achieve IND-CCA2 security.

  • Key derivation uses SHAKE-256 (XOF) and SHA3-512 throughout.

  • Encapsulation key (public key) and decapsulation key (private key) renamed from Kyber conventions.

docs.title: 3.3.1 Specification Summary
docs.text:
FIPS 204 standardizes ML-DSA (based on CRYSTALS-Dilithium), a Fiat-Shamir signature scheme with rejection sampling to prevent secret leakage.

Key design choices:

  • Modulus \(q = 8380417 = 2^{23} - 2^{13} + 1\) (NTT-friendly prime).

  • Polynomial degree \(n = 256\), supporting efficient NTT.

  • Rejection sampling ensures signatures reveal no information about the secret key.

  • Message hashing via SHAKE-256; deterministic signing by default in FIPS 204.

  • Three variants: ML-DSA-44 (Level 2), ML-DSA-65 (Level 3), ML-DSA-87 (Level 5).

docs.title: 3.5 HQC: The Fifth PQC Standard
docs.text:
NIST selected HQC (Hamming Quasi-Cyclic) in March 2025 as the fifth PQC algorithm and the second KEM standard. HQC provides:

  • Diversity: Backup to lattice-based ML-KEM, based on code-based hard problems (not lattices).

  • Different mathematical foundation: If a breakthrough attack on MLWE is found, HQC remains secure.

  • Moderate key sizes: \(\sim\)2–7 KB public keys (much more practical than Classic McEliece’s 1.3 MB).

A draft FIPS for HQC is expected in 2025–2026.

docs.text:

Table 3.5. NIST IR 8547 Algorithm Transition Timeline Algorithm Current Use Deprecated Disallowed RSA (all key sizes) Key exchange, signatures 2030 2035 ECDH (all curves) Key exchange 2030 2035 ECDSA (all curves) Digital signatures 2030 2035 DH (classic) Key exchange 2030 2035 DSA Digital signatures 2023 (already) 2030 ECDH P-256 TLS key exchange 2030 2035 ECDSA P-384 Certificate signing 2030 2035 AES-128 Symmetric encryption Not deprecated Retain w/ PQC SHA-256 Hashing Not deprecated Retain

Action Required Before 2030

Systems using RSA, ECDH, ECDSA, or DH must migrate to NIST PQC standards (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) before 2030. For systems with long-lived keys or sensitive data, migration should begin immediately due to the HNDL threat.

docs.title: 3.9 FIPS 140-3 and Algorithm Compliance
docs.text:
FIPS 140-3 is the U.S. government standard for cryptographic module validation (CMVP — Cryptographic Module Validation Program):

  • All FIPS-approved modules must use only FIPS 140-3 approved algorithms.

  • ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA are FIPS 140-3 approved as of 2024–2025.

  • Cryptographic modules must be validated by NIST-accredited labs (cost: $50K–$500K, timeline: 12–24 months).

  • Security Level 1–4 validation, with Level 2/3 requiring physical security.

CMVP Status 2025

As of early 2025, several implementations of ML-KEM and ML-DSA have undergone or are undergoing FIPS 140-3 CMVP validation. Key vendors: AWS (AWS-LC), Microsoft (SymCrypt), Botan, wolfSSL, OpenSSL (via providers). Check NIST’s CMVP module search at csrc.nist.gov/projects/cryptographic-module-validation-program.

docs.title: 3.11 Summary
docs.text:
• FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) are the three finalized NIST PQC standards as of August 2024.

  • HQC was selected in March 2025 as the fifth algorithm, adding code-based algorithmic diversity.

  • NIST IR 8547 mandates deprecation of RSA, ECDH, ECDSA by 2030 and disallowance by 2035.

  • NSA CNSA 2.0 requires ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87 (Level 5) for classified systems with earlier deadlines.

  • FN-DSA (FALCON) is expected in FIPS 206 for applications requiring compact signatures.

  • 14 additional signature candidates are under evaluation; MAYO and SNOVA are among the most promising.

docs.title: 4.1.1 liboqs — Open Quantum Safe
docs.text:
liboqs is the primary open-source C library for PQC, developed by the Open Quantum Safe (OQS) project. It provides a unified API for all NIST-standardized algorithms plus many candidates.

#include <oqs/oqs.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main(void) {
    OQS_KEM *kem = OQS_KEM_new(OQS_KEM_alg_ml_kem_768);
    if (kem == NULL) { fprintf(stderr, "KEM init failed\n"); return 1; }

    uint8_t *pk = malloc(kem->length_public_key);    /* 1184 bytes */
    uint8_t *sk = malloc(kem->length_secret_key);    /* 2400 bytes */
    uint8_t *ct = malloc(kem->length_ciphertext);    /* 1088 bytes */
    uint8_t *ss_enc = malloc(kem->length_shared_secret); /* 32 bytes */
    uint8_t *ss_dec = malloc(kem->length_shared_secret);

    /* Key generation */
    OQS_STATUS rc = OQS_KEM_keypair(kem, pk, sk);
    if (rc != OQS_SUCCESS) goto cleanup;

    /* Encapsulation (sender) */
    rc = OQS_KEM_encaps(kem, ct, ss_enc, pk);
    if (rc != OQS_SUCCESS) goto cleanup;

    /* Decapsulation (receiver) */
    rc = OQS_KEM_decaps(kem, ss_dec, ct, sk);
    if (rc != OQS_SUCCESS) goto cleanup;

    printf("Shared secrets match:
           memcmp(ss_enc, ss_dec, kem->length_shared_secret) == 0
           ? "YES" : "NO");

cleanup:
    OQS_KEM_free(kem);
    free(pk); free(sk); free(ct); free(ss_enc); free(ss_dec);
    return rc == OQS_SUCCESS ? 0 : 1;
}

#include <oqs/oqs.h>

int pqc_sign_verify_example(void) {
    OQS_SIG *sig = OQS_SIG_new(OQS_SIG_alg_ml_dsa_65);

    uint8_t *pk = malloc(sig->length_public_key);   /* 1952 bytes */
    uint8_t *sk = malloc(sig->length_secret_key);   /* 4000 bytes */
    uint8_t *signature = malloc(sig->length_signature); /* <=3309 B */
    size_t sig_len;

    const uint8_t *message = (uint8_t*)"Hello PQC World!";
    size_t msg_len = 16;

    OQS_SIG_keypair(sig, pk, sk);
    OQS_SIG_sign(sig, signature, &sig_len, message, msg_len, sk);
    OQS_STATUS valid = OQS_SIG_verify(sig, message, msg_len,
                                       signature, sig_len, pk);

    printf("Signature valid:
           valid == OQS_SUCCESS ? "YES" : "NO");

    OQS_SIG_free(sig);
    free(pk); free(sk); free(signature);
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 4.1.2 OQS Provider for OpenSSL
docs.text:
The OQS provider integrates PQC into OpenSSL 3.x, enabling PQC in TLS, X.509 certificates, and all OpenSSL-based applications:

# Install OQS Provider
git clone https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider.git
cd oqs-provider
cmake -S . -B build -DOPENSSL_ROOT_DIR=/usr/local/ssl
cmake --build build
sudo cmake --install build

# Configure OpenSSL to load OQS provider
# In openssl.cnf:
# [provider_sect]
# default = default_sect
# oqsprovider = oqsprovider_sect
# [oqsprovider_sect]
# activate = 1

# Generate ML-KEM-768 keypair
openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-KEM-768 -out mlkem768_key.pem

# Generate ML-DSA-65 certificate
openssl req -new -x509 -nodes \
    -newkey ML-DSA-65 \
    -keyout mldsa65_key.pem \
    -out mldsa65_cert.pem \
    -subj "/CN=PQC Test CA"

# TLS server with PQC
openssl s_server -cert mldsa65_cert.pem -key mldsa65_key.pem \
    -groups mlkem768 -port 4433

# TLS client with PQC
openssl s_client -connect localhost:4433 -groups mlkem768

# List available PQC algorithms
openssl list -kem-algorithms -provider oqsprovider
openssl list -signature-algorithms -provider oqsprovider

docs.title: 4.1.5 mlkem-native: Formally Verified Implementation
docs.text:
mlkem-native is a production-quality, formally verified implementation of ML-KEM with:

  • CBMC formal verification: Memory safety, no undefined behavior, functional correctness.

  • Optimized backends: AARCH64 and x86_64 (AVX2) assembly for critical inner loops.

  • Constant-time: Verified constant-time NTT and arithmetic operations.

  • Integrated: Used in AWS-LC and Microsoft SymCrypt.

docs.title: 4.2 Hardware Acceleration
docs.text: Hardware acceleration is essential for high-throughput and low-latency PQC deployments (TLS servers, HSMs, embedded systems).

docs.title: 4.2.1 NTT Hardware Architecture
docs.text:
The Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) is the computational bottleneck of lattice-based PQC. An optimized NTT hardware unit provides \(10\times\)–\(100\times\) speedup over software.

Figure 4.1. NTT butterfly unit: core computation for lattice-based PQC hardware.

A complete NTT hardware accelerator for ML-KEM (\(n=256\), \(q=3329\)) requires:

  • 8 layers of \(n/2=128\) butterfly operations each.

  • Each butterfly: one modular multiplication + two modular additions.

  • Twiddle factor ROM: \(256 \times 12\) bits \(= 384\) bytes.

#include <cupqc.h>

docs.title: 4.3.2 Assembly Optimization Techniques
docs.text:
The Cortex-M4’s UMAAL (Unsigned Multiply Accumulate Accumulate Long) instruction is critical for modular arithmetic:

/* Cortex-M4 Montgomery modular multiplication using UMAAL */
/* Computes a*b*R^-1 mod q, where R = 2^32 */
static inline uint32_t montgomery_mul(uint32_t a, uint32_t b,
                                       uint32_t q, uint32_t q_inv) {
    uint32_t lo, hi;
    uint64_t result;
    uint32_t m;

    /* Inline assembly using UMAAL for double-precision */
    __asm__ volatile (
        "umull
        "mul
        "umlal
        : [lo]"=r"(lo), [hi]"=r"(hi), [m]"=r"(m)
        : [a]"r"(a), [b]"r"(b), [q]"r"(q), [qi]"r"(q_inv)
    );
    return hi;  /* hi is the Montgomery result */
}

docs.title: 4.3.4 On-the-Fly Key Expansion
docs.text:
For ultra-constrained devices (RAM \(< 4\)KB), the public matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) can be expanded on-the-fly from its seed rather than stored:

/* Instead of storing A[k][k][256] (requires k*k*256*2 bytes = ~3KB for k=3)
 * generate each row on-the-fly during matrix-vector multiplication */
void matvec_onthefly(poly *result, const uint8_t *seed, const poly *vec,
                     int k, bool transposed) {
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
        poly_init(&result[i]);
        for (int j = 0; j < k; j++) {
            poly a_ij;
            /* Generate single polynomial from seed with indices */
            gen_poly_from_seed(&a_ij, seed, transposed ? j : i,
                               transposed ? i : j);
            poly_ntt_mul_acc(&result[i], &a_ij, &vec[j]); /* += A_ij * vec_j */
        }
    }
}
/* Memory savings: ~3KB for k=3 vs storing entire matrix */

• liboqs provides a comprehensive unified API for all NIST PQC algorithms in C.

  • OQS Provider integrates PQC into OpenSSL 3.x for TLS, X.509, and all OpenSSL-based applications.

  • mlkem-native offers formally verified, production-quality ML-KEM with assembly optimizations.

  • NTT acceleration (FPGA/ASIC) achieves \(<\)10\(\mu\)s per ML-KEM operation; GPU achieves 1M ops/sec.

  • pqm4 provides optimized Cortex-M4 implementations; ML-KEM-768 KeyGen requires \(\sim\)764 kcc.

  • On-the-fly key expansion significantly reduces RAM usage for ultra-constrained IoT devices.

  • Bouncy Castle (Java), Rust crates, and Go’s cloudflare/circl provide idiomatic PQC across languages.

docs.title: 5.1 Why Migration Is Urgent
docs.text:
The transition to post-quantum cryptography is not a future concern — it is an active imperative for any organization handling data with long-term sensitivity. The “Harvest Now, Decrypt Later” threat means that adversaries are collecting encrypted traffic today for future decryption.

The Migration Urgency Matrix

Prioritize migration based on data sensitivity and system lifetime:

  • Critical: Classified data, long-lived PKI roots, financial records \(>\)10 years — migrate now

  • High: Healthcare data, government infrastructure, defence systems — migrate by 2026

  • Medium: Enterprise data, customer PII, internal communications — migrate by 2028

  • Lower: Short-lived session keys, public content — migrate before 2030

docs.title: 5.2 The NIST NCCoE Migration Framework
docs.text:
NIST’s National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE) published SP 1800-38 (“Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography”) defining a five-phase framework:

Figure 5.1. NIST NCCoE SP 1800-38 PQC migration framework.

docs.title: 5.2.1 Phase 1: Cryptographic Inventory (Discovery)
docs.text:
Identify all cryptographic assets in the organization:

  1. Application discovery: Enumerate all applications using cryptography.

  2. Protocol analysis: Find all TLS, SSH, IPsec, S/MIME deployments.

  3. Certificate inventory: Catalog X.509 certificates (keys, algorithms, expiry dates).

  4. Key management: Document HSMs, key stores, key derivation.

  5. Data classification: Which data is sensitive for 10+ years?

  6. Third-party dependencies: Vendor libraries, SDKs, cloud services using classical crypto.

docs.title: 5.2.2 Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM)
docs.text:
A CBOM is a structured inventory of all cryptographic assets, analogous to a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM):

  "cbom_version": "1.4",
  "metadata": {"component": "payment-service", "version": "3.2.1"},

      "replacement": "ML-KEM-768",

      "retention_years": 7
    },
    {

      "notes": "Retain; quantum-safe"

}

CBOM tools: Microsoft Cryptography Scanner, IBM’s Crypto Inventory, NIST’s NCCoE tools, Cryptosense Analyzer, PQShield PQAdvisor.

docs.title: 5.2.3 Phase 2: Risk Assessment
docs.text:
For each cryptographic asset, assess:

  1. Quantum Vulnerability: Does it use RSA, ECDH, ECDSA, or DH? If yes, it’s vulnerable.

  2. Data Sensitivity: Is the protected data sensitive beyond 10 years?

  3. HNDL Exposure: Is the data transmitted over untrusted networks (internet, satellite)?

  4. Migration Complexity: How hard is it to replace this component? Custom HSM firmware? Vendor dependency?

  5. Interconnected Systems: Which other systems depend on this cryptographic component?

docs.title: 5.3 Crypto-Agility
docs.text: Crypto-agility is the ability to quickly replace cryptographic algorithms without major system redesign. It is the key architectural principle for long-term PQC resilience.

docs.title: 5.3.1 Crypto-Agility Design Patterns
docs.text:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from enum import Enum
import oqs  # liboqs Python wrapper

class KEMAlgorithm(Enum):
    ECDH_P256 = "ECDH-P256"
    ML_KEM_768 = "ML-KEM-768"
    ML_KEM_1024 = "ML-KEM-1024"
    X25519_MLKEM768 = "X25519MLKEM768"   # Hybrid

class KEMProvider(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def keygen(self) -> tuple[bytes, bytes]: ...    # (public, private)
    @abstractmethod
    def encapsulate(self, pk: bytes) -> tuple[bytes, bytes]: ...  # (ct, ss)
    @abstractmethod
    def decapsulate(self, sk: bytes, ct: bytes) -> bytes: ...     # ss

class LiboqsKEM(KEMProvider):
    def __init__(self, alg: str):
        self.kem = oqs.KeyEncapsulation(alg)

    def keygen(self):
        pk = self.kem.generate_keypair()
        return pk, self.kem.export_secret_key()

    def encapsulate(self, pk: bytes):
        ct, ss = self.kem.encap_secret(pk)
        return ct, ss

    def decapsulate(self, sk: bytes, ct: bytes):
        return self.kem.decap_secret(ct)

class KEMFactory:
    _registry: dict[str, type] = {}

    @classmethod
    def register(cls, name: str, provider: type):
        cls._registry[name] = provider

    @classmethod
    def create(cls, alg: KEMAlgorithm) -> KEMProvider:
        name = alg.value
        if name not in cls._registry:
            # Default to liboqs for PQC algorithms
            return LiboqsKEM(name)
        return cls._registry[name]()

# Usage -- algorithm can be changed by config, not code
config_kem = KEMAlgorithm.X25519_MLKEM768   # From config file
kem = KEMFactory.create(config_kem)
pk, sk = kem.keygen()
ct, ss = kem.encapsulate(pk)

docs.title: 5.4.1 TLS 1.3 Migration
docs.text:
TLS 1.3 migration requires updating both key exchange (KEM) and authentication (signature):

  1. Key Exchange: Replace ECDHE with X25519MLKEM768 (hybrid) or ML-KEM-768 (pure PQC).

  2. Server Certificate: Replace RSA/ECDSA with ML-DSA-65 or SLH-DSA.

  3. Client Authentication: Update client certificates if mutual TLS is used.

# /etc/nginx/nginx.conf (with OQS-enabled OpenSSL)
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/mldsa65.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/mldsa65.key;

    # Prefer hybrid PQC, fallback to classical
    ssl_ecdh_curve      X25519MLKEM768:x25519:prime256v1;

    # Require TLS 1.3 only
    ssl_protocols       TLSv1.3;

    # Modern cipher suite (AES-256 for PQC era)
    ssl_ciphers         TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384:TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256;
}

docs.title: 5.4.2 SSH Migration
docs.text:
# OpenSSH 9.0+ supports ML-KEM hybrid key exchange
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config (server)
KexAlgorithms mlkem768x25519-sha256,curve25519-sha256,ecdh-sha2-nistp256

# Client connection with PQC KEM
ssh -o KexAlgorithms=mlkem768x25519-sha256 user@server

# Generate ML-DSA host key (when supported)
ssh-keygen -t mldsa65 -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_mldsa65_key

docs.title: 5.4.3 PKI and X.509 Migration
docs.text:
The PKI migration is the most complex aspect, involving certificate hierarchies:

  1. Root CA: Generate new ML-DSA-87 root CA (highest security level).

  2. Intermediate CAs: New ML-DSA-65 intermediate CAs under PQC root.

  3. End-entity certificates: Issue ML-DSA-65 certificates for servers and clients.

  4. Cross-certification: Run parallel classical + PQC hierarchies during transition.

  5. OCSP/CRL: Ensure revocation infrastructure supports PQC.

  6. HSM update: Upgrade or replace HSMs to support PQC key generation.

# Generate ML-DSA-87 root CA private key
openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-DSA-87 -out root_ca_key.pem \
    -provider oqsprovider -provider default

# Self-signed root CA certificate (10-year validity)
openssl req -new -x509 -key root_ca_key.pem \
    -out root_ca.pem \
    -days 3650 \
    -subj "/CN=PQC Root CA/O=Example Corp/C=US" \
    -extensions v3_ca \
    -provider oqsprovider -provider default

# Generate ML-DSA-65 intermediate CA
openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-DSA-65 -out int_ca_key.pem \
    -provider oqsprovider -provider default

openssl req -new -key int_ca_key.pem \
    -out int_ca.csr \
    -subj "/CN=PQC Intermediate CA/O=Example Corp"

# Sign with root CA
openssl x509 -req -in int_ca.csr \
    -CA root_ca.pem -CAkey root_ca_key.pem \
    -out int_ca.pem -days 1825 \
    -provider oqsprovider -provider default

docs.title: 5.4.4 Dual-Certificate Approach
docs.text:
During the transition, running classical and PQC certificates in parallel maintains compatibility:

# nginx dual-certificate configuration
server {
    listen 443 ssl;

    # Classical certificate (for legacy clients)
    ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/ecdsa_p384.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/ecdsa_p384.key;

    # PQC certificate (for PQC-capable clients)
    ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/mldsa65.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/mldsa65.key;

    # TLS will automatically negotiate using the client's capability
    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
    ssl_ecdh_curve X25519MLKEM768:x25519:prime256v1;
}

docs.title: 5.7 Summary
docs.text:
• The HNDL threat makes PQC migration urgent today, not when CRQCs arrive.

  • The NIST NCCoE SP 1800-38 framework provides a practical 5-phase migration methodology.

  • Cryptographic inventory (CBOM) is the essential first step — you cannot protect what you don’t know.

  • Crypto-agility (algorithm-agnostic design patterns) enables rapid algorithm replacement.

  • Hybrid PQC (X25519MLKEM768) is the recommended transition approach for TLS: security against both classical and quantum attackers with backward compatibility.

  • PKI migration is the most complex piece: start with root CA updates and plan for dual-certificate operation.

  • NIST IR 8547 mandates RSA/ECDH/ECDSA deprecated by 2030 and disallowed by 2035.

docs.title: 6.1 Rationale for Hybrid Cryptography
docs.text:
Hybrid cryptography combines a classical algorithm with a post-quantum algorithm in a single key exchange or signature scheme. The core security argument:

Hybrid Security Guarantee

A hybrid scheme is secure if either the classical or the PQC component is secure. If a breakthrough attack on MLWE is found, the classical ECDH component maintains security against classical attackers. If a CRQC becomes available, the PQC component maintains security against quantum attackers. This “belt and suspenders” approach is the recommended transition strategy.

Figure 6.1. Hybrid KEM construction: combining classical and PQC shared secrets via KDF.

docs.title: 6.2 Generic Hybrid KEM Construction
docs.text:
The standard hybrid KEM construction follows RFC 9180 (HPKE) combined with IETF draft for hybrid PQC:

Algorithm: Hybrid KEM Construction

  1. KeyGen:

  2. \((ek_1, dk_1) \leftarrow \text{KEM}_1\text{.KeyGen}()\) // Classical (e.g., X25519)

  3. \((ek_2, dk_2) \leftarrow \text{KEM}_2\text{.KeyGen}()\) // PQC (e.g., ML-KEM-768)

  4. return \((ek = ek_1 \| ek_2, \; dk = dk_1 \| dk_2)\)

  5. Encapsulate\((ek)\):

  6. \((K_1, ct_1) \leftarrow \text{KEM}_1\text{.Encaps}(ek_1)\)

  7. \((K_2, ct_2) \leftarrow \text{KEM}_2\text{.Encaps}(ek_2)\)

  8. \(K \leftarrow \text{HKDF-SHA256}(K_1 \| K_2, ct_1 \| ct_2 \| ek)\)

  9. return \((K, \; ct = ct_1 \| ct_2)\)

  10. Decapsulate\((dk, ct)\):

  11. \(K_1 \leftarrow \text{KEM}_1\text{.Decaps}(dk_1, ct_1)\)

  12. \(K_2 \leftarrow \text{KEM}_2\text{.Decaps}(dk_2, ct_2)\)

  13. \(K \leftarrow \text{HKDF-SHA256}(K_1 \| K_2, ct_1 \| ct_2 \| ek)\)

  14. return \(K\)

The KDF combiner ensures that the combined key \(K\) is indistinguishable from random if either \(K_1\) or \(K_2\) is a uniformly random string. This provides the hybrid security guarantee.

docs.title: 6.3 X25519MLKEM768 — The Recommended Hybrid
docs.text:
X25519MLKEM768 is the specific hybrid KEM standardized in IETF drafts and already deployed by major browsers and CDNs:

Table 6.1. X25519MLKEM768 Key Sizes Component Element Classical PQC / Total X25519 Public key 32 bytes — ML-KEM-768 Encapsulation key — 1184 bytes Combined Public key total 32 B 1216 bytes X25519 Ciphertext 32 bytes — ML-KEM-768 Ciphertext — 1088 bytes Combined Ciphertext total 32 B 1120 bytes Combined Shared secret 32+32 B 32 B (after KDF)

docs.title: 6.3.1 TLS Overhead Analysis
docs.text:
Table 6.2. TLS 1.3 Key Exchange Overhead: Classical vs Hybrid vs PQC Method ClientHello (B) ServerHello (B) Extra RTT Security X25519 (classical) 32 32 0 Classical only X25519MLKEM768 (hybrid) 1216 1120 0 Classical + PQC ML-KEM-768 (pure PQC) 1184 1088 0 PQC only

The additional overhead of X25519MLKEM768 over classical X25519 is \(\sim\)2 KB per TLS handshake, adding negligible latency (\(<\)1ms) on modern networks.

docs.title: 6.4.1 Signal’s PQXDH (Post-Quantum Extended Diffie-Hellman)
docs.text:
Signal Protocol adopted PQXDH (2023) as the first widely deployed PQC messaging protocol:

  1. Pre-key bundle: Each device publishes an ML-KEM-1024 encapsulation key alongside classical X25519 keys.

  2. Initial message: Sender encapsulates to both the classical X25519 and ML-KEM-1024 keys.

  3. Key derivation: Combined shared secret via HKDF, then used to initialize Double Ratchet.

  4. Forward secrecy: Post-quantum forward secrecy is achieved by the ephemeral ML-KEM key per session.

docs.title: 6.4.2 Apple iMessage PQ3 (2024)
docs.text:
Apple’s PQ3 protocol for iMessage provides post-quantum protection at security level 3 (highest level Apple has deployed):

  • ML-KEM-768 hybrid key exchange for initial session establishment.

  • Periodic ML-KEM re-keying to limit exposure of stored messages.

  • ML-DSA-65 for device identity authentication.

  • Backward-compatible with existing iMessage infrastructure.

  • Deployed February 2024, protecting over 1 billion iMessage users.

docs.title: 6.4.3 Meta Messenger E2EE
docs.text:
Meta’s end-to-end encrypted Messenger (2024) uses hybrid PQC:

  • Key exchange: X25519 + CRYSTALS-Kyber (predecessor to ML-KEM) hybrid.

  • Authentication: ECDSA + ML-DSA hybrid signatures for device keys.

docs.title: 6.5 Hybrid Signatures
docs.text: Hybrid signatures combine classical and PQC signature schemes for the transition period:

docs.title: 6.5.1 Composite Signatures (X.509)
docs.text:
The IETF “composite crypto” drafts define hybrid X.509 certificates with dual signatures:

# Generate composite keypair: ML-DSA-65 + ECDSA P-384
openssl genpkey -algorithm id-MLDSA65-ECDSA-P384-SHA384 \
    -out composite_key.pem \
    -provider oqsprovider -provider default

# Self-signed composite certificate
openssl req -new -x509 \
    -key composite_key.pem \
    -out composite_cert.pem \
    -days 3650 \
    -subj "/CN=Hybrid PQC Server" \
    -provider oqsprovider -provider default

# The certificate contains TWO signature values:
# 1. ML-DSA-65 signature (PQC-resistant)
# 2. ECDSA-P384 signature (classical, for legacy compatibility)
openssl x509 -in composite_cert.pem -text | grep "Signature Algorithm"

docs.title: 6.5.2 Concatenated Hybrid Signatures
docs.text:
An alternative approach concatenates the two signatures:

\[\sigma_{\text{hybrid}} = \sigma_{\text{classical}} \| \sigma_{\text{PQC}} \| \text{len}(\sigma_{\text{classical}})\]

Verification requires both signatures to be valid (OR semantics provide security if either is secure against its threat model).

docs.title: 6.6 Hybrid KDF Security Analysis
docs.text:
The security of the hybrid KDF combiner depends on the construction:

Table 6.4. Hybrid Combiner Options Combiner Construction Security Standard XOR \(K = K_1 \oplus K_2\) Weak; only safe if both uniform Avoid Concatenation+KDF \(K = \text{HKDF}(K_1 \| K_2, …)\) Strong IETF draft Split KDF \(K_1' = \text{KDF}(K_1), K_2' = \text{KDF}(K_2), K = K_1' \oplus K_2'\) Strong RFC 8470

HKDF Hybrid Combiner Best Practice

Use: \(K = \text{HKDF}(K_1 \| K_2, \; ct_1 \| ct_2 \| ek_1 \| ek_2, \;\text{“hybrid-kem”})\)

Including the ciphertexts and public keys in the HKDF info field prevents “ciphertext binding” attacks where an adversary substitutes part of the hybrid ciphertext.

docs.title: 6.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Hybrid cryptography provides a “belt and suspenders” security guarantee: secure if either component is secure.

  • X25519MLKEM768 is the recommended hybrid KEM, already deployed in Chrome, Firefox, and Cloudflare.

  • The TLS overhead of hybrid PQC is \(\sim\)2 KB per handshake — negligible for most applications.

  • Signal’s PQXDH and Apple’s PQ3 demonstrate successful large-scale hybrid PQC deployments.

  • HKDF is the correct combiner for hybrid KEMs; XOR-only combiners are insecure.

  • Composite X.509 certificates with dual signatures (classical + PQC) enable PKI migration without breaking legacy clients.

  • Hybrid PQC is the recommended transition strategy for 2025–2030; pure PQC becomes the target post-2030.

docs.title: 7.1 Overview of PQC Testing
docs.text:
Testing PQC implementations requires multiple complementary approaches:

  1. Known Answer Tests (KAT): Verify functional correctness against reference vectors.

  2. NIST ACVP: Automated Cryptographic Validation Protocol for FIPS validation.

  3. Interoperability testing: Cross-implementation compatibility.

  4. Performance benchmarking: Cycle counts, latency, throughput.

  5. Fuzzing and memory safety: Security testing for implementation bugs.

  6. Formal verification: Mathematical proof of correctness.

  7. Side-channel testing: Physical security validation (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 7.2 Known Answer Tests (KAT)
docs.text: KAT vectors are the primary method for verifying algorithm implementations against NIST reference implementations.

docs.title: 7.2.1 KAT Format
docs.text:

git clone https://github.com/PQClean/PQClean.git
cd PQClean

# Build and run ML-KEM-768 KAT test

python3 test/test_pqclean.py --kem ml-kem-768 ml-kem-512 ml-kem-1024

docs.title: 7.2.3 KAT Testing with liboqs
docs.text:
import oqs
import binascii

def verify_kat_vector(kat_file: str, algorithm: str) -> bool:
    """Verify implementation against NIST KAT vectors."""
    kem = oqs.KeyEncapsulation(algorithm)

    with open(kat_file) as f:
        lines = f.readlines()

    passed = failed = 0
    i = 0
    while i < len(lines):
        if lines[i].startswith('seed = '):
            seed = bytes.fromhex(lines[i].split(' = ')[1].strip())
            pk_ref = bytes.fromhex(lines[i+1].split(' = ')[1].strip())
            sk_ref = bytes.fromhex(lines[i+2].split(' = ')[1].strip())
            ct_ref = bytes.fromhex(lines[i+3].split(' = ')[1].strip())
            ss_ref = bytes.fromhex(lines[i+4].split(' = ')[1].strip())

            # Set deterministic seed
            oqs.randombytes_custom_algorithm(seed)
            pk = kem.generate_keypair()
            ct, ss_enc = kem.encap_secret(pk)
            ss_dec = kem.decap_secret(ct)

            if pk == pk_ref and ct == ct_ref and ss_enc == ss_ref:
                passed += 1
            else:
                print(f"FAIL at seed {binascii.hexlify(seed[:8])!r}")
                failed += 1
            i += 5
        else:
            i += 1

    print(f"KAT {algorithm}: {passed} passed, {failed} failed")
    return failed == 0

docs.text:
import time
import statistics
import oqs

def benchmark_kem(algorithm: str, iterations: int = 1000):
    """Benchmark a KEM algorithm: keygen, encaps, decaps."""
    kem = oqs.KeyEncapsulation(algorithm)

    keygen_times, encaps_times, decaps_times = [], [], []

    for _ in range(iterations):
        # KeyGen
        t0 = time.perf_counter_ns()
        pk = kem.generate_keypair()
        keygen_times.append(time.perf_counter_ns() - t0)

        # Encapsulate
        t0 = time.perf_counter_ns()
        ct, ss = kem.encap_secret(pk)
        encaps_times.append(time.perf_counter_ns() - t0)

        # Decapsulate
        t0 = time.perf_counter_ns()
        ss2 = kem.decap_secret(ct)
        decaps_times.append(time.perf_counter_ns() - t0)

        assert ss == ss2, "Shared secret mismatch!"

    def stats(times):
        med = statistics.median(times)
        return f"{med/1000:.1f}μs (median), {min(times)/1000:.1f}μs (min)"

    print(f"\n=== {algorithm} (n={iterations}) ===")
    print(f"  KeyGen:  {stats(keygen_times)}")
    print(f"  Encaps:  {stats(encaps_times)}")
    print(f"  Decaps:  {stats(decaps_times)}")
    print(f"  pk: {len(pk)}B, ct: {len(ct)}B, ss: {len(ss)}B")

# Run benchmarks
for alg in ["ML-KEM-512", "ML-KEM-768", "ML-KEM-1024"]:
    benchmark_kem(alg)

#include <oqs/oqs.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stddef.h>
#include <string.h>

/* libFuzzer entry point */
int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(const uint8_t *data, size_t size) {
    OQS_KEM *kem = OQS_KEM_new(OQS_KEM_alg_ml_kem_768);
    if (!kem) return 0;

    /* Only proceed if we have enough data for a secret key */
    if (size < kem->length_secret_key) {
        OQS_KEM_free(kem);
        return 0;
    }

    /* Use fuzz input as the secret key */
    const uint8_t *sk = data;

    /* Use remainder as ciphertext (padded/truncated to correct size) */
    uint8_t ct[1088] = {0};  /* ML-KEM-768 ciphertext size */
    size_t ct_data_len = size - kem->length_secret_key;
    memcpy(ct, data + kem->length_secret_key,
           ct_data_len < sizeof(ct) ? ct_data_len : sizeof(ct));

    uint8_t ss[32];
    /* Should never crash or abort -- just return error/implicit rejection */
    OQS_KEM_decaps(kem, ss, ct, sk);

    OQS_KEM_free(kem);
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 8.1 Side-Channel Attack Overview
docs.text:
Side-channel attacks extract secret information from the physical implementation of a cryptographic algorithm, rather than attacking the mathematical structure. Even mathematically secure algorithms can be completely broken by side-channel attacks.

Figure 8.1. Side-channel attack taxonomy.

docs.title: 8.2.1 Timing Attacks
docs.text:
Timing attacks measure the execution time of cryptographic operations to infer secret values.

Variable-Time Code is Dangerous

Any code path that depends on secret data — branches, memory accesses, division operations — can leak timing information. This is especially dangerous in:

  • Comparison functions (must use constant-time comparison)

  • Rejection sampling (FALCON signature is particularly vulnerable)

  • Polynomial coefficient operations with data-dependent control flow

docs.title: Example: Dangerous vs Safe Comparison
docs.text:
/* DANGEROUS: Early exit leaks length of matching prefix */
int bad_compare(const uint8_t *a, const uint8_t *b, size_t len) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        if (a[i] != b[i]) return 0;  // Timing reveals mismatch position!
    }
    return 1;
}

/* SAFE: Constant-time comparison -- no early exit */
int ct_compare(const uint8_t *a, const uint8_t *b, size_t len) {
    volatile uint8_t result = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        result |= (a[i] ^ b[i]);  // Always processes all bytes
    }
    return result == 0;  /* 1 if equal, 0 if different */
}

/* BEST: Use libsodium or liboqs built-in constant-time memcmp */
#include <sodium.h>  /* or */
#include <oqs/common.h>
int secure = (0 == sodium_memcmp(a, b, len));
int secure2 = OQS_MEM_secure_compare(a, b, len); /* liboqs */

docs.title: 8.2.2 Simple Power Analysis (SPA)
docs.text: SPA examines a single power trace to identify operations. An attacker observing the power waveform of a device can distinguish NTT operations, multiplication sequences, and control flow.

docs.title: 8.2.3 Differential Power Analysis (DPA)
docs.text:
DPA uses statistical analysis of many power traces to recover secret keys, even with noise:

  1. Collect \(N\) traces \(t_i\) paired with known inputs \(x_i\).

  2. For each key hypothesis \(k\): compute predicted intermediate value \(v_i = f(x_i, k)\).

  3. Compute the correlation between predicted \(v_i\) and measured traces \(t_i\).

  4. The correct key hypothesis produces the highest correlation.

docs.title: 8.2.4 Electromagnetic (EM) Attacks
docs.text: Near-field EM probes can capture localized EM emanations from specific circuits on a chip, sometimes enabling attacks even when power traces are difficult to obtain. EM attacks are particularly effective against FPGAs and embedded processors.

docs.title: 8.2.5 Cache-Timing Attacks
docs.text:
Cache-timing attacks exploit timing differences caused by cache hits vs. misses:

/* VULNERABLE: Table lookup with secret index (cache timing leak) */
uint8_t sbox[256];  /* Initialization omitted */
uint8_t bad_substitution(uint8_t secret_index) {
    return sbox[secret_index];  /* Cache miss if sbox[secret_index] not cached! */
}

/* SAFE: Constant-time table lookup using bitwise operations */
uint8_t ct_table_lookup(const uint8_t *table, size_t table_len,
                         uint8_t secret_index) {
    uint8_t result = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < table_len; i++) {
        /* Select table[i] if i == secret_index, else 0 */
        uint8_t mask = (uint8_t)(-(uint8_t)(i == secret_index));
        result |= mask & table[i];  /* No branch, no cache timing */
    }
    return result;
}

docs.title: 8.2.6 Fault Injection Attacks
docs.text: Fault injection attacks intentionally introduce faults (voltage glitches, laser pulses, clock glitches) to cause incorrect computation, then analyze the erroneous output.

docs.title: Fault Attack on ML-KEM Decapsulation
docs.text:
ML-KEM’s decapsulation includes a re-encryption check to verify ciphertext validity. If this check is bypassed via fault injection:

  1. Attacker sends modified ciphertext \(c' = c \oplus \Delta\) with a single-bit error.

  2. Normal: decapsulation detects modification via re-encryption check, returns implicit rejection.

  3. With fault: re-encryption check is skipped; decapsulation returns information about \(c'\).

  4. An attacker who receives the erroneous output can recover the secret.

/* FIPS 203 Decaps: always re-encrypt and compare in constant time */
int mlkem_decaps(uint8_t *ss, const uint8_t *ct, const uint8_t *dk) {
    uint8_t m_prime[32];
    uint8_t ct_prime[CIPHERTEXT_LEN];
    uint8_t K_bar[32];

    /* Step 1: Decrypt to get m' */
    mlkem_decrypt(m_prime, ct, dk);

    /* Step 2: ALWAYS re-encrypt (no early exit, no branch on result) */
    mlkem_encrypt_deterministic(ct_prime, m_prime, dk + OFFSET_H, &K_bar);

    /* Step 3: Constant-time comparison of original vs re-encrypted ct */
    int match = ct_compare(ct, ct_prime, CIPHERTEXT_LEN); /* ct_compare is CT */

    /* Step 4: Select K or K_bar based on match result (constant-time select) */
    volatile uint8_t mask = (uint8_t)(-(int8_t)match); /* 0xFF if match */
    for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) {
        ss[i] = (mask & m_prime[i]) | (~mask & K_bar[i]); /* CT select */
    }
    return 0;  /* Always return 0; never signal failure via return value */
}
/* Note: In FIPS 203, ss is always returned (implicit rejection) */

docs.title: 8.3.2 ML-DSA Side-Channel Considerations
docs.text:
ML-DSA’s rejection sampling is a critical source of side-channel leakage:

  1. The number of rejections before accepting a signature is secret-dependent.

  2. Measuring signing time reveals information about the signing randomness.

  3. Countermeasure: Use deterministic signing (hedge signing with entropy) and mask the number of iterations.

docs.title: 8.3.3 FALCON (FN-DSA) Critical Vulnerability
docs.text:
FALCON uses Gaussian sampling over the integers with floating-point arithmetic, which is particularly vulnerable:

FALCON FP Arithmetic is a Security Critical Issue

FALCON’s Gaussian sampler uses floating-point (FP) double-precision arithmetic. On many microprocessors:

  • FP operations are not constant-time (denormal numbers, FPU exceptions)

  • Timing of FP division and square root varies with input values

  • This creates exploitable timing channels for private key recovery

Secure FALCON implementation requires either: (1) emulated FP with constant-time guarantees, or (2) dedicated hardware support. The mlkem-native approach uses table-based Gaussian sampling that avoids FP arithmetic entirely.

docs.title: 8.4.1 Masking
docs.text:
Masking splits secret values into random shares to prevent statistical correlation attacks:

/* Boolean masking: split secret 's' into shares s0, s1 where s = s0 XOR s1 */
typedef struct { uint16_t s0, s1; } MaskedCoeff;

MaskedCoeff mask_coefficient(uint16_t s, uint16_t random_mask) {
    MaskedCoeff m;
    m.s1 = random_mask;         /* Random mask (share 1) */
    m.s0 = s ^ random_mask;     /* Share 0 = s XOR mask */
    return m;
}

/* Masked multiplication: computes a*b where b is masked */
/* (a * b) = (a * b.s0) XOR (a * b.s1) */
MaskedCoeff masked_mul_q(uint16_t a, MaskedCoeff b, uint16_t q) {
    MaskedCoeff result;
    uint16_t new_mask = get_random_uint16();
    result.s1 = new_mask;
    result.s0 = ((uint32_t)a * b.s0 + (uint32_t)a * b.s1)
    /* Note: Full masked NTT requires more sophisticated approach */
    return result;
}

docs.title: 8.4.2 Randomization
docs.text:
/* Blinded NTT: multiply input by random invertible element before NTT,
 * divide after. Prevents power analysis of specific coefficient positions. */
void blinded_ntt(uint16_t *poly, size_t n, uint16_t q) {
    /* Step 1: Generate random blinding factor r (invertible mod q) */
    uint16_t r, r_inv;
    do {
        r = oqs_rand_uint16()
    } while (r == 0 || !mod_inverse_exists(r, q, &r_inv));

    /* Step 2: Blind polynomial: poly[i] *= r (mod q) */
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        poly[i] = (uint32_t)poly[i] * r
    }

    /* Step 3: Standard NTT */
    ntt(poly, n, q);

    /* Step 4: Remove blinding: poly[i] *= r_inv (mod q) */
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        poly[i] = (uint32_t)poly[i] * r_inv
    }
}

docs.title: 8.5.1 TVLA (Test Vector Leakage Assessment)
docs.text:
TVLA is the standard methodology for assessing side-channel leakage:

  1. Two groups: Group A (fixed input) and Group B (random inputs).

  2. Power traces: Collect \(N\) traces from each group.

  3. Welch’s t-test: Compute \(t\)-statistic comparing the two trace distributions.

  4. Decision threshold: \(|t| > 4.5\) at any time sample indicates leakage.

  5. First-order TVLA detects linear leakage; higher-order TVLA detects masked leakage.

docs.title: 8.6 Tools for SCA Research
docs.text:
Table 8.4. Open-Source Side-Channel Analysis Tools Tool Language Capabilities ChipWhisperer Python/C Capture power/EM; CW-Nano, CW-Pro hardware; TVLA SCALib Python Statistical SCA library; SNR, TVLA, profiled attacks Inspector (Riscure) Java Commercial; full DPA/DFA suite scared Python Side-channel analysis library; aligned trace processing lascar Python Trace analysis; DPA, CPA; GPU-accelerated 
import numpy as np
from scalib.metrics import SNR
from scipy import stats

def tvla_first_order(traces_fixed: np.ndarray,
                      traces_random: np.ndarray,
                      threshold: float = 4.5) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    First-order TVLA: Welch's t-test comparing fixed vs random input traces.
    Returns t-statistic for each time sample.
    """
    # Welch's t-test (unequal variance)
    t_values, _ = stats.ttest_ind(traces_fixed, traces_random,
                                   equal_var=False, axis=0)

    # Find leaking samples
    leaking = np.abs(t_values) > threshold
    n_leaking = np.sum(leaking)

    if n_leaking > 0:
        print(f"WARNING: {n_leaking} leaking time samples detected!")
        print(f"Max |t| = {np.max(np.abs(t_values)):.2f} (threshold={threshold})")
    else:
        print(f"PASS: No leakage detected. Max |t| = {np.max(np.abs(t_values)):.2f}")

    return t_values

docs.title: 8.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Side-channel attacks are practical threats to PQC implementations, independent of mathematical security.

  • Timing attacks exploit variable-time execution; use constant-time primitives throughout.

  • DPA/EM attacks exploit power/EM correlations with secret data; masking is the primary countermeasure.

  • Fault injection attacks can bypass security checks; always use constant-time, branch-free security checks.

  • ML-KEM requires constant-time comparison in decapsulation; FIPS 203 mandates implicit rejection (always returns output, never branches on decryption failure).

  • FALCON’s floating-point Gaussian sampler is a critical implementation challenge; requires special care or hardware support.

  • TVLA (via tools like ChipWhisperer + SCALib) is the standard methodology for evaluating side-channel leakage.

  • FIPS 140-3 Level 3/4 requires physical side-channel countermeasures for hardware security modules.

docs.title: Chapter 9: PQC Applications and National Solutions
9.1 TLS and Secure Web Communication
docs.text: TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the most widely deployed cryptographic protocol. Migrating TLS to PQC protects web, API, VPN, and data-center traffic.

docs.title: 9.1.1 TLS 1.3 with PQC
docs.text:
TLS 1.3’s clean design (fixed cipher suites, single key exchange) makes PQC integration straightforward:

# /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/pqc-server.conf
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name pqc.example.com;

    # ML-DSA-65 server certificate and key
    ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/certs/server_mldsa65.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/private/server_mldsa65_key.pem;

    # TLS 1.3 only; include hybrid PQC key exchange
    ssl_protocols TLSv1.3;
    ssl_ecdh_curve X25519MLKEM768:x25519:prime256v1;

    # Cipher suites (AES-256 preferred for PQC era)
    ssl_ciphers TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384:TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256;

    # OCSP stapling for certificate revocation
    ssl_stapling on;
    ssl_stapling_verify on;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://backend;
        add_header X-PQC-KEM X25519MLKEM768 always;
    }
}

Cloudflare has been the largest early deployer of PQC at scale:

  • Deployed X25519MLKEM768 by default on all Cloudflare edge servers (2024).

  • Over 50% of TLS connections to Cloudflare now use PQC key exchange.

  • Conducted measurement studies showing negligible performance impact (\(<\)0.5% latency increase).

docs.title: 9.2.1 Signal’s PQXDH Protocol

docs.title: 9.2.2 Apple iMessage PQ3
