Apple PQ3 (February 2024) provides Level 3 post-quantum security:

  • Initial session: ML-KEM-768 hybrid with X25519 for initial key exchange.

  • Periodic re-keying: ML-KEM encapsulation in every message re-establishes forward secrecy.

  • Authentication: ECDSA + ML-DSA composite signatures on device keys.

  • Reach: Protects over 1 billion iMessage users by default since iOS 17.4.

docs.title: 9.3.1 X.509 PQC Certificates
docs.text:
PQC certificates have significantly different sizes from classical certificates:

Table 9.1. X.509 Certificate Size Comparison Algorithm Public Key (B) Sig (B) Cert size (B) Chain (B) RSA-2048 256 256 \(\approx\)1000 \(\approx\)4000 ECDSA P-256 64 64 \(\approx\)500 \(\approx\)2000 ML-DSA-44 1312 2420 \(\approx\)4200 \(\approx\)12000 ML-DSA-65 1952 3309 \(\approx\)5800 \(\approx\)17000 SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f 32 17088 \(\approx\)17700 \(\approx\)52000

Certificate Size Impact

ML-DSA-65 certificates are \(\sim\)10\(\times\) larger than ECDSA P-256. This impacts TLS handshake performance (more data transmitted) but is well within acceptable limits for most applications. SLH-DSA’s large signatures may cause issues in protocols with size limits.

docs.title: 9.3.2 Certificate Transparency (CT) Impact
docs.text: Larger PQC certificates also increase the storage and bandwidth requirements for Certificate Transparency logs. CT log operators are planning infrastructure upgrades for the PQC era.

docs.title: 9.4 Code Signing
docs.text:
Code signing with PQC protects against quantum-enabled code tampering:

import oqs
import hashlib
import json
import os

def sign_artifact(artifact_path: str, sk_path: str, output_path: str):
    """Sign a file artifact with SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f."""
    # Read artifact and compute its hash
    with open(artifact_path, 'rb') as f:
        data = f.read()
    artifact_hash = hashlib.sha256(data).digest()

    # Create signing metadata
    metadata = {
        "file": os.path.basename(artifact_path),
        "size": len(data),
        "sha256": artifact_hash.hex(),
        "algorithm": "SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f",
        "version": "1.0"
    }
    msg = json.dumps(metadata, sort_keys=True).encode()

    # Load private key and sign
    with open(sk_path, 'rb') as f:
        sk = f.read()

    signer = oqs.Signature("SPHINCS+-SHA2-128f-simple")  # SLH-DSA
    signature = signer.sign(msg, sk)

    # Write signature bundle
    bundle = {
        "metadata": metadata,
        "signature": signature.hex()
    }
    with open(output_path, 'w') as f:
        json.dump(bundle, f, indent=2)
    print(f"Signed {artifact_path} -> {output_path}")
    print(f"Signature size: {len(signature)} bytes")

def verify_artifact(artifact_path: str, bundle_path: str, pk_path: str):
    """Verify a PQC-signed artifact."""
    with open(artifact_path, 'rb') as f:
        data = f.read()
    with open(bundle_path) as f:
        bundle = json.load(f)
    with open(pk_path, 'rb') as f:
        pk = f.read()

    # Verify hash
    actual_hash = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()
    assert actual_hash == bundle["metadata"]["sha256"], "Hash mismatch!"

    # Reconstruct signed message
    msg = json.dumps(bundle["metadata"], sort_keys=True).encode()
    sig = bytes.fromhex(bundle["signature"])

    # Verify signature
    verifier = oqs.Signature("SPHINCS+-SHA2-128f-simple")
    is_valid = verifier.verify(msg, sig, pk)
    print(f"Signature {'VALID' if is_valid else 'INVALID'}")
    return is_valid

docs.title: 9.5.1 Bitcoin and ECDSA Vulnerability
docs.text:
Bitcoin uses ECDSA over secp256k1 for transaction signing. A CRQC running Shor’s algorithm could:

  1. Derive private key from public key in polynomial time.

  2. Sign fraudulent transactions on behalf of any address that has revealed its public key.

  3. Addresses that have never transacted (public key not revealed) are safer, but transacted addresses are vulnerable.

docs.title: 9.5.2 Quantum Resistant Ledger (QRL)
docs.text:
QRL is the first proof-of-work blockchain using PQC natively:

  • Uses XMSS (eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme) for all transaction signing.

  • Stateful key management: each QRL wallet manages XMSS tree state.

  • Proof-of-Work consensus with XMSS-signed blocks.

  • Fully operational since 2018.

docs.title: 9.6 National and Indigenous PQC Solutions
docs.text: Countries and regions have developed indigenous PQC cryptographic standards and algorithms alongside (or instead of) NIST standards.

docs.title: 9.6.1 China: SM-Series Cryptography
docs.text:
China’s commercial cryptographic standards are managed by the State Cryptography Administration (SCA, or OSCCA):

Table 9.2. China SM Cryptographic Standards Standard Type Description Status SM2 ECC Signature/KEM 256-bit elliptic curve; used in Chinese PKI Mandatory for gov. SM3 Hash 256-bit hash function; similar to SHA-256 Mandatory SM4 Block cipher 128-bit key, 128-bit block; replace AES Mandatory SM9 Identity-based Pairing-based identity-based encryption Optional ZUC Stream cipher SNOW-based; used in LTE/5G Telecom standard

China’s PQC research: CNITSEC (National Research Center for Information Technology Security) is actively developing indigenous PQC algorithms. SM2/SM9 are quantum-vulnerable; China is expected to announce indigenous PQC standards from their national standardization body.

docs.title: 9.6.2 Russia: GOST Cryptographic Standards
docs.text:
Russia’s GOST (state standard) cryptographic algorithms are managed by the Federal Security Service (FSB):

Table 9.3. Russian GOST Cryptographic Standards Standard Type Description GOST R 34.10-2012 ECC Signature 256/512-bit elliptic curve signatures (quantum-vulnerable) GOST R 34.11-2012 (Streebog) Hash 256/512-bit hash function GOST R 34.12-2015 (Grasshopper/Magma) Block cipher 128-bit and 64-bit block ciphers GOST R 34.13-2015 Block cipher modes Cipher modes of operation

Russia’s ViPNet (InfoWatch) and Crypto-Pro companies are developing PQC extensions to GOST. GOST R 34.10-2012 is quantum-vulnerable and will require replacement.

docs.title: 9.6.3 South Korea: KPQC
docs.text:
South Korea’s National Intelligence Service (NIS) and KISA (Korea Internet & Security Agency) conducted the Korean PQC (KPQC) competition (2022–2024):

Table 9.4. Korean PQC (KPQC) Algorithm Finalists Algorithm Type Description Level Status HAETAE Lattice Sig Module-lattice signature (Korean design) 2/3/5 Selected NTRUplus Lattice KEM NTRU-based KEM (Korean design) 1/3/5 Selected Peregrine Lattice Sig FALCON variant (Korean enhanced) 1/3/5 Selected PALOMA Code KEM Code-based KEM (similar to Classic McEliece) 1/3/5 Selected SOLMAE Lattice Sig Module-NTRU signature scheme 2/3 Selected

KPQC winners are expected to become Korean domestic standards in 2025–2026 alongside NIST standards.

docs.title: 9.6.4 Germany: BSI (Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik)
docs.text:
BSI provides comprehensive PQC guidance:

  • Technical Guideline TR-02102-1: Specifies approved cryptographic mechanisms.

  • Updated 2024 to include ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA as approved algorithms.

  • BSI recommends hybrid PQC as the current best practice.

  • BSI mandates SLH-DSA for long-lived signatures (\(>\)10 years), ML-DSA for general use.

  • ELSI: BSI’s quantum-safe initiative for critical infrastructure.

docs.title: 9.6.5 France: ANSSI (Agence Nationale de la Sécurité des Systèmes d’Information)
docs.text:
ANSSI PQC position (2024):

  • Endorses NIST PQC standards while advocating for European evaluation.

  • Recommends hybrid classical+PQC for the transition period.

  • Published “Recommandations pour la migration vers la cryptographie post-quantique” (2024).

  • ANSSI emphasizes the importance of European PQC research and standards development.

  • Collaborates with ENISA (European Union Agency for Cybersecurity) on EU-wide PQC guidance.

docs.title: 9.6.6 Japan: CRYPTREC
docs.text:
Japan’s CRYPTREC (Cryptography Research and Evaluation Committees) manages Japanese cryptographic standards:

  • Updated the CRYPTREC cipher list to include PQC algorithms (2024).

  • Monitoring NIST PQC standards and IPA (Information-technology Promotion Agency) conducting PQC evaluation.

  • Japan’s NICT (National Institute of Information and Communications Technology) conducting research on lattice-based and hash-based PQC.

docs.title: 9.6.7 India
docs.text:
India’s PQC developments:

  • C-DAC (Centre for Development of Advanced Computing): Developing PQC reference implementations for Indian e-governance applications.

  • CERT-In: Issued advisories on PQC migration for government departments.

  • STQC (Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification): Evaluating PQC for FIPS-equivalent Indian standards.

  • India’s National Cyber Security Policy 2020 emphasizes indigenous cryptographic capability development.

docs.title: 9.6.8 Australia: ASD (Australian Signals Directorate)
docs.text:
Australia’s ASD PQC guidance:

  • Published “Post-Quantum Cryptography” guidance aligned with NSA CNSA 2.0.

  • Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC) recommends ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 for general use.

  • ASD participates in Five Eyes (FVEY) PQC coordination: USA, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand.

  • NCSC (UK), CISA (US), CCCS (Canada) jointly published PQC transition guidance.

docs.title: 9.6.9 Israel
docs.text:
Israel’s PQC activities:

  • NIMDA (Israel National Cyber Directorate) issued PQC transition guidelines.

  • WeizmanInstitute, Ben-Gurion University, Hebrew University active in PQC research.

  • Strong industry presence: Ironclad, Ceva Wireless PQC IP cores, SIEVERT.

docs.title: 9.7.1 DTLS 1.3 with PQC for IoT
docs.text:
DTLS (Datagram TLS) is used for UDP-based IoT communication. PQC DTLS implementations:

Table 9.5. PQC DTLS Implementation Feasibility for IoT Classes Device Class RAM Feasible PQC Approach High-end IoT (RPi, ESP32-S3) \(>\)512 KB All NIST PQC Full stack Mid-range (STM32F4, nRF5340) 256–512 KB ML-KEM-768, ML-DSA-44 pqm4 or liboqs Low-end (STM32L0, nRF52832) 64–256 KB ML-KEM-512 PQClean, on-the-fly Ultra-constrained (\(<\)64 KB) \(<\)64 KB ML-KEM-512 (marginal) Custom optimization

docs.title: 9.7.2 Automotive: V2X and Secure Boot
docs.text:
Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication uses ECDSA (IEEE 1609.2) for authentication. PQC migration path:

  • V2X certificates: Migrate from ECDSA P-256 to ML-DSA-44 (IEEE 1609.2 PQC extension in development).

  • Secure boot: Replace ECDSA-signed firmware with ML-DSA-signed firmware.

  • HSM integration: Automotive HSMs (e.g., SHE, AUTOSAR SecOC) require PQC hardware support.

  • Vehicle lifetime of 15+ years means cars built today may face CRQC attacks before retirement.

docs.title: 9.8 Summary
docs.text:
• TLS is the most urgent migration target; X25519MLKEM768 hybrid is already deployed by Chrome, Firefox, and Cloudflare.

  • Signal (PQXDH) and Apple iMessage (PQ3) demonstrate successful PQC deployment for secure messaging.

  • PQC X.509 certificates are 5–30\(\times\) larger than ECDSA equivalents; infrastructure must be updated.

  • Bitcoin/blockchain systems using ECDSA are quantum-vulnerable; QRL demonstrates a PQC-native ledger.

  • China (SM-series), Russia (GOST), South Korea (KPQC), Germany (BSI), and Japan (CRYPTREC) are developing indigenous PQC standards and guidance.

  • Korea’s KPQC selected HAETAE, NTRUplus, Peregrine, PALOMA, and SOLMAE as domestic candidates.

  • IoT devices can implement ML-KEM-512 even on constrained platforms (\(>\)64 KB RAM).

  • Automotive V2X communication requires PQC migration due to 15+ year vehicle lifetimes.

docs.title: Chapter 10: PQC Research and Open Problems
10.1 Open Security Problems
docs.text: Despite the NIST standardization of PQC algorithms, significant open security questions remain.

docs.title: BKZ Algorithm Progress
docs.text:
The BKZ (Block Korkine-Zolotarev) algorithm is the primary classical algorithm for solving lattice problems. Its practical efficiency determines PQC security levels.

Table 10.1. BKZ Performance and Lattice Security Estimates Year BKZ Development Impact on Security Estimates Reference 1987 BKZ original Baseline lattice reduction Schnorr-Euchner 2011 BKZ 2.0 Preprocessing with “tours”; \(\sim\)20% efficiency gain Chen-Nguyen 2016 G6K sieve GPU-accelerated sieving; faster BKZ oracle Ducas et al. 2021 Filtered PNJ-BKZ Progressive BDGL sieving; tighter analysis Ducas et al. 2024 Chen et al. (preprint) Improved quantum enumeration; re-analysis of RLWE security Under review

2024 Chen et al. Preprint

In 2024, a preprint by Chen, Zhang, and colleagues claimed improved attacks on RLWE-based systems. After initial review, the community found the analysis was partially correct but did not break current NIST parameters. The incident highlighted the ongoing need for conservative parameter selection and continuous security analysis. NIST parameters include significant security margins above current best attacks.

docs.title: Module Structure and Security
docs.text: An open question: does the module structure of MLWE (vs. plain LWE) introduce exploitable structure? Current analysis suggests module structure is either as hard as or only slightly easier than plain LWE with equivalent parameters, but this is an active research area.

docs.title: 10.1.2 Code-Based Security Gaps
docs.text:
• ISD improvements: Information Set Decoding algorithms (Prange, Stern, BJMM, MMT, DOOM) continue to improve. HQC parameters are designed with 10–15 bit security margin over current best ISD.

  • Quasi-cyclic structure: Does the quasi-cyclic structure of HQC codes introduce algebraic weaknesses beyond SDP? Research ongoing.

  • Decoding failure probability: Any non-zero decoding failure rate in a KEM can be exploited; HQC’s parameters target \(2^{-128}\) failure probability.

docs.title: 10.1.3 Isogeny-Based Security After SIDH
docs.text:
Post-SIDH isogeny research focuses on:

  • CSIDH security: The GAIP (Group Action Inverse Problem) underlying CSIDH — quantum security analysis still evolving. Recent attacks suggest CSIDH-512 provides only \(\sim\)73-bit quantum security.

  • SQIsign security: Based on non-linear hidden path problem; believed hard for quantum computers, but proof is elusive.

  • Higher-dimensional extensions: SQIsignHD uses degree-2\(^k\) isogenies to speed up SQIsign but introduces new security assumptions.

docs.title: 10.2.1 Threshold PQC
docs.text:
Threshold signatures allow \(t\)-of-\(n\) parties to jointly sign without any single party holding the complete secret key:

  • FROST-ML-DSA: Threshold variant of ML-DSA; active IETF draft.

  • TECDSA-PQC: Classical TECDSA extended with PQC components.

  • Applications: Multi-party signing for blockchain, HSM backup, cloud KMS.

  • Challenge: Rejection sampling in ML-DSA complicates threshold constructions.

docs.title: 10.2.2 Zero-Knowledge Proofs from PQC
docs.text:
ZK-SNARKs and other zero-knowledge proof systems classically use pairings (BLS12-381), which are quantum-vulnerable. PQC ZK alternatives:

Table 10.2. Post-Quantum Zero-Knowledge Proof Systems System Basis Description Proof size Status FAEST AES-MPC AES circuit in MPC-in-the-head 5–6 KB NIST R2 candidate Banquet AES-MPC 3-party AES OWF; smaller proof 17 KB Research Picnic LowMC-MPC MPC-in-the-head from LowMC 12–40 KB Mature STARK Hash Scalable transparent; no trusted setup 300+ KB Deployed Dilithium-G Lattice ZK proofs of ML-DSA signature knowledge 10+ KB Research

docs.title: 10.2.3 Quantum-Safe Key Derivation
docs.text:
Key derivation functions (KDFs) and key agreement protocols require analysis for quantum safety:

  • HKDF with ML-KEM: HKDF-SHA256 remains quantum-safe (Grover gives 128-bit security with 256-bit outputs).

  • PQC in TLS 1.3 KDF: The TLS 1.3 handshake KDF (HKDF) is quantum-safe; only key exchange needs PQC upgrade.

  • Session key independence: Each TLS session uses a fresh ML-KEM key; compromise of one session does not affect others.

docs.title: 10.2.4 Blockchain and Post-Quantum Consensus
docs.text:
• Ethereum’s PQC roadmap: Ethereum (post-Merge) uses BLS12-381 for validator signatures (quantum-vulnerable). The Ethereum roadmap includes a PQC transition, estimated 2030+.

  • PQC-friendly VRFs: Verifiable Random Functions for PoS consensus need PQC versions; lattice-based VRFs under research.

  • PQC STARKs for scaling: STARKs (hash-based, quantum-safe) already deployed for Ethereum L2 scaling (StarkNet, Polygon zkEVM).

docs.title: 10.3 Quantum Computing Progress
docs.text:
Understanding the actual timeline of CRQC development is critical for migration planning.

Table 10.3. Quantum Computing Milestones (2019–2025) Year Organization Milestone Qubits 2019 Google “Quantum supremacy” — Sycamore (random circuit sampling) 53 2021 IBM Eagle processor 127 2022 IBM Osprey processor 433 2023 IBM Condor + Heron processors 1121 2024 Google Willow chip — below-threshold error correction 105 2025 IBM “Quantum-centric supercomputing” roadmap updates 4000+

CRQC Timeline Estimates

  • Near-term (now–2030): No CRQC capable of breaking RSA-2048. Current devices too noisy and small. However, HNDL risk is real.

  • Medium-term (2030–2035): Potential emergence of early CRQCs with limited capability. NIST deprecation deadline.

  • Long-term (2035+): High probability of full CRQCs. All classical public-key cryptography at risk.

  • Key metric: Breaking RSA-2048 with Shor’s algorithm requires \(\sim\)4000 logical qubits with fault tolerance \(\sim 10^{-12}\), requiring millions of physical qubits. Current devices: 1000–4000 physical qubits with error rates \(\sim 10^{-3}\).

docs.title: 10.4 Post-Quantum Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC)
docs.text:
MPC allows multiple parties to jointly compute a function without revealing their inputs. Classical MPC uses:

  • Oblivious Transfer (OT) based on LWE — already PQC-secure.

  • Garbled circuits based on AES — quantum-safe with AES-256.

  • Secret sharing (Shamir) based on information-theoretic security — inherently quantum-safe.

Key open problems in PQC MPC:

  1. Efficient PQC-based OT extensions (replacing Diffie-Hellman based OT).

  2. PQC-friendly commitments for MPC protocols.

  3. Threshold FALCON signing without floating-point complications.

docs.title: 10.5.1 Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) from Lattices
docs.text:
ABE allows decryption based on attributes (“decrypt if age \(>\) 18 AND country = US”). Lattice-based ABE:

  • Boneh-Boyen-Gentry (BBG) ABE is quantum-vulnerable (pairing-based).

  • LWE-based ABE schemes exist but are significantly larger and slower.

  • Garg-Gentry-Halevi-Raykova (GGHR) provides lattice ABE with bounded attributes.

docs.title: 10.5.2 Functional Encryption from Lattices
docs.text:
Functional encryption allows computing arbitrary functions on encrypted data:

  • Inner-product FE: Well-studied from LWE (ABDP scheme, 2020).

  • General FE: Constructible from indistinguishability obfuscation (iO), which has lattice constructions but is extremely inefficient.

  • Applications: Encrypted analytics, privacy-preserving ML.

docs.title: 10.5.3 Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
docs.text:
FHE, introduced by Gentry in 2009, allows computation on encrypted data. All practical FHE schemes are lattice-based:

Table 10.4. FHE Schemes and Libraries (2024–2025) Scheme Basis Best For Library BFV RLWE Integer arithmetic; exact computation SEAL (Microsoft) BGV RLWE Integer arithmetic; batching HEAAN, HElib CKKS RLWE Approximate real arithmetic; ML SEAL, OpenFHE TFHE LWE Boolean circuits; fast bootstrapping TFHE, Concrete FHEW LWE Boolean; gate-by-gate FHEW

FHE performance (2025): TFHE performs \(\sim\)10,000 boolean gates/second on GPU; CKKS achieves \(\sim\)10 ms per 1024-element vector multiplication. Still 100–10,000\(\times\) slower than plaintext computation, but advancing rapidly.

docs.title: 10.7 Security Estimation: lattice-estimator
docs.text:
The lattice-estimator is the standard tool for estimating the concrete security of lattice-based schemes:

# Install: pip install lattice-estimator
from estimator import *
from estimator.lwe_parameters import LWEParameters
from estimator import ND  # noise distributions

# ML-KEM-768 parameters (MLWE, k=3, n=256, q=3329, eta=2)
# Analyze as equivalent LWE with n_eff = k*n = 768
params_mlkem768 = LWEParameters(
    n=768,         # Effective dimension
    q=3329,        # Modulus
    Xs=ND.CenteredBinomial(2),  # Secret distribution (eta=2)
    Xe=ND.CenteredBinomial(2),  # Error distribution (eta=2)
    m=768+32,      # Number of LWE samples (public key + ciphertext)
    tag="ML-KEM-768"
)

# Run all standard attacks
print("=== ML-KEM-768 Security Estimates ===")
result = LWE.estimate(params_mlkem768, deny_list=["arora-gb"])

# Print best attack cost
for attack, cost in result.items():
    print(f"  {attack}: {cost.get('rop', '?'):.1f} bit security")

# Expected output (approximately):
# ML-KEM-768 Security Estimates:
#   usvp: 174.3 bit security
#   dual: 171.8 bit security
#   dual_hybrid: 168.4 bit security
# All > 160 bits classical security -> Level 3 confirmed

docs.title: 10.9 Summary and Future Outlook
docs.text:
• Lattice security analysis continues: BKZ improvements, module structure questions, quantum enumeration improvements require ongoing monitoring.

  • The 2024 Chen et al. preprint demonstrated that community scrutiny is essential; NIST parameter margins provide important safety buffers.

  • Isogeny-based cryptography (SQIsign, CSIDH) remains promising for ultra-compact keys but awaits maturity.

  • Threshold PQC, zero-knowledge proofs, and attribute-based encryption from lattices are major active research frontiers.

  • FHE (lattice-based) is advancing rapidly; practical deployments for medical data analysis, ML inference expected by 2027–2030.

  • CRQC timeline: No CRQC before 2030, high risk 2030–2035, near-certain by 2040. HNDL means action is required now.

  • South Korea’s KPQC, Chinese national standards, and European research programs demonstrate global investment in PQC.

  • The lattice-estimator, G6K sieve tools, and IACR ePrint are essential resources for tracking the security state of PQC algorithms.

Final Recommendation

The field of post-quantum cryptography has matured from theoretical research to concrete deployable standards. The NIST standards (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, and HQC) represent the current best available algorithms with well-analyzed security margins. The time to migrate is now: deploy hybrid PQC for internet-facing services, begin cryptographic inventory, update PKI infrastructure, and build crypto-agile systems that can adapt to future algorithm changes. The quantum threat is not science fiction — it is an engineering problem with a known solution.
